```{r library}
library(masque)
```

## Why

A field agronomist has a confidential 72-plot trial and wants an outside
statistician to build a spatial yield model on it, without the statistician
seeing the real yields or genotype names. This vignette shows the
agronomist's side of that handover on the John and Williams (1995)
alpha-design trial shipped with the package.

The synthetic table is a copy for writing code, meant for a named
collaborator and not for public release. *Confidentiality and the threat
model* sets out what is and is not protected. Read it before sharing any
output.

## What

`masque()` is the main function. Point it at a table, or a folder or
workbook of related tables, and it reads the data, proposes a masking
plan and masks. In an interactive session it pauses first so the
data owner can review the plan.

The output of `masque()` is a pair: the *synthetic* clone, the only part
that crosses the trust boundary, and a private `masque_recipe` (see
`recipe()`) that stays on the data owner's machine. With the recipe, a
pipeline written on the synthetic table later runs on the original without
changes. *Recipe anatomy and the round-trip* covers what the recipe holds
and the functions that use it.

Every column in the masking plan has a `role` and an `action`, proposed by
`propose_roles()` and changed with `set_role()`. The role says what the
column is: `design`, `treatment`, `outcome`, `covariate`, `date`, `id`,
`text` or `other`. The action says what happens to it:

* `keep` passes it through unchanged.
* `noise` replaces it with independent draws that use nothing from its
  values beyond a coarse summary.
* `scramble` re-simulates numerics through a Gaussian copula and shuffles
  categories and dates between rows. For a treatment it swaps the labels
  among the levels, so the allocation is unchanged.
* `alias` replaces the labels with opaque codes. A categorical covariate
  is shuffled between rows first.
* `drop` leaves it out.

### What a default clone keeps

By default, every outcome and covariate is simulated independently. Each
numeric column keeps only its approximate range and shape. Only the
experimental design and the pattern of missing values are kept exactly, and
labels are replaced by codes.

In more detail, the default clone:

* keeps every design column's structure exactly. Categorical design labels
  become codes such as `block_D001`, and numeric design columns such as
  row, column or plot number are kept as they are.
* replaces treatment labels with codes such as `trt_001`. Each plot keeps
  its treatment.
* draws each numeric outcome and covariate, and each date column,
  independently from a distribution built on the column's 1st percentile,
  deciles and 99th percentile. Every value lies between the 1st and 99th
  percentiles, apart from the rounding that keeps whole numbers whole.
* draws each categorical covariate uniformly over its levels, relabelled as
  codes such as `soil_L001`. A logical column is drawn uniformly over the
  values it holds.
* draws a column that is constant within a design unit, such as a
  site-level rainfall, once per unit.
* is audited for leakage when it is made.
* keeps the missing values in the same cells, and each column's storage
  class.
* drops columns that look like identifiers (by name, such as `plot_id`),
  columns whose names suggest personal information (`email`, `phone`,
  `owner`), free text (a character column in which more than half the
  values are distinct) and columns of a class `masque` cannot simulate.

Beyond the design and the treatment allocation, it keeps no relationship
between columns, including the one between treatment and outcome, so it
holds no real effect for a model to find. Use
it to write and run a pipeline, not to tune one.

### Opting into structure

The `mode` argument chooses the defaults for every column at once. The
default is `"null"`, described above. Two other modes keep more:

* `"local"` is for the data owner's own development. Labels stay as they
  are, identifiers and text are kept, and numerics are re-simulated
  through a Gaussian copula with empirical marginals, which keeps each
  column's distribution and the correlations between numeric columns.
  A local clone must not leave the data owner's machine.
* `"collaborate"` is for a clone shared with someone else. It simulates
  numerics as `"local"` does and jitters them, replaces treatment and
  categorical covariate labels with codes (design labels stay, apart from
  a detected environment), drops identifiers and free text, and runs the
  leakage audit (`audit_mask()`, which grades each column HIGH, medium or
  low) when the clone is made.

Only these two modes accept `conditional = TRUE`, which mimics the
treatment effect (see *Confidentiality and the threat model*). A
per-column `action` always overrides the mode's default.

## Example

### The one-call path

```{r one-call}
f <- system.file("extdata", "john_alpha.csv", package = "masque")
df <- read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
knitr::kable(
  head(df),
  caption = "The first six plots of the alpha-design trial."
)
```

```{r one-call-mask}
m <- masque(df, seed = 1L, ask = FALSE)
```

`ask = FALSE` skips the interactive review, as a vignette must. In an
interactive console, `masque(df)` shows the proposed plan and asks whether
to proceed, edit or stop. The messages above are the summary `masque()`
prints for every guided run: the mode, the number of columns masked and
the leakage-audit tally.

The result carries the synthetic data and the private recipe:

```{r one-call-extract}
synth <- synthetic(m)
knitr::kable(
  head(synth),
  caption = paste0(
    "The first six plots of the default clone: `rep`, `block` and `gen` ",
    "are replaced by codes, and `yield` is drawn independently."
  )
)
```

The plot layout is unchanged, each real block maps to one coded block, and
every synthetic yield lies between the 1st and 99th percentiles of the
real yields:

```{r one-call-checks}
identical(synth$plot, df$plot) && identical(synth$row, df$row) &&
  identical(synth$col, df$col)
codes_per_block <- tapply(as.character(synth$block), df$block, function(x) {
  length(unique(x))
})
all(codes_per_block == 1L)
range(synth$yield)
quantile(df$yield, c(0.01, 0.99))
```

### A clone with structure

When the pipeline needs the relationships between columns, ask for them
with a mode. A collaborate clone of the same trial re-simulates yield
through the copula and runs the leakage audit before it is shared. With
only one numeric column, this trial has no correlation for the copula to
keep, so the visible difference is that the design labels stay:

```{r one-call-collaborate}
m_collab <- masque(df, mode = "collaborate", seed = 2L, ask = FALSE)
knitr::kable(
  head(synthetic(m_collab)),
  caption = paste0(
    "The first six plots of a collaborate clone: design labels are kept, ",
    "`gen` is replaced by codes, and `yield` is re-simulated."
  )
)
```

The masking plan each mode proposes for this trial:

```{r plan-modes}
plan_null <- propose_roles(df)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    col = plan_null$col,
    role = plan_null$role,
    null = plan_null$action,
    local = propose_roles(df, mode = "local")$action,
    collaborate = propose_roles(df, mode = "collaborate")$action
  ),
  caption = "The action each mode proposes for each column of the trial."
)
```

### The masking plan: roles and actions

Under the one-call path, `masque()` built the roles table without asking.
Building it yourself lets you review and change it first:

```{r plan}
plan <- propose_roles(df)
knitr::kable(
  plan[, c("col", "role", "action", "kind")],
  caption = "The proposed masking plan for the alpha-design trial."
)
```

`propose_roles()` proposes an action for each column for the chosen mode,
so the table reviewed here is the plan that will run. A roles table
remembers the mode it was built for, and `mask()` uses that mode unless
told otherwise. `yield` was proposed as the trial's `outcome` from its
name. In a default clone the outcome role changes nothing. A conditional clone
(see *Confidentiality and the threat model*) uses it to find the response.
Any role can be changed with `set_role()`. Here `plot` is given the role
`id`, which the default drops:

```{r set-role}
plan_id <- set_role(plan, "plot", role = "id")
knitr::kable(
  plan_id[, c("col", "role", "action")],
  caption = "The plan with `plot` as an identifier."
)
```

Changing a role resets the action to that role's default, unless you also
pass `action`. Naming an outcome is optional. Outcomes and numeric
covariates are re-simulated together either way, and only a conditional
clone reads the outcome role.

### Editing the plan as code

The plan is a data.table, so you can edit it in code. The spreadsheet
editor that opens when the data owner chooses `e` at the guided prompt
edits the same table.
`set_role()` is vectorised over columns:

```{r edit-vectorised}
r2 <- set_role(plan, c("row", "col"), action = "drop")
```

Direct edits work too. A direct `role` edit leaves `action` untouched, so
setting the action to `NA` tells `mask()` to fill in the default for the
new role:

```{r edit-direct}
r2[col == "rep", `:=`(role = "covariate", action = NA_character_)]
knitr::kable(
  r2[, c("col", "role", "action")],
  caption = paste0(
    "A hand-edited plan: `row` and `col` dropped, `rep` made a ",
    "covariate."
  )
)
```

The `kind` column comes from the column's class and cannot be edited. If
it is wrong, convert the column in the data and run `propose_roles()`
again.

`role_options()` lists the pairs the package accepts, here for a factor
column:

```{r role-options}
knitr::kable(
  role_options(kind = "factor")[, c("role", "action")],
  caption = paste0(
    "Every (role, action) pair the validator accepts for a factor ",
    "column."
  )
)
```

The plan also has a `pii_suspected` column. `propose_roles()` sets it
from the column *name* (`email`, `phone`, `owner`, ...) and drops a
flagged column in every mode. If a flagged column is kept, the audit
grades it HIGH. The scan reads names, not content, so flag or drop a
harmlessly named column that holds sensitive values, such as a `paddock`
column holding farm names:

```{r pii-by-hand, eval = FALSE}
plan[col == "paddock", pii_suspected := TRUE]
```

Passing a plan to `mask()`, or to `masque(df, roles = plan)`, runs it.
Here is the proposed plan as it stands:

```{r mask}
m <- mask(df, plan, seed = 1L)
synth <- synthetic(m)
byte_identical_plot <- identical(synth$plot, df$plot)
gen_levels_changed <- !setequal(levels(synth$gen), levels(df$gen))
byte_identical_plot
gen_levels_changed
head(levels(synth$gen))
```

### A plan the package refuses

`plot` is a `design` column. Scrambling it would break the trial's layout,
and `mask()` refuses:

```{r fail-closed, error = TRUE}
bad_plan <- set_role(plan, "plot", role = "design", action = "scramble")
mask(df, bad_plan, seed = 1L)
```

The call stops before any masking, names the column and the combination at
fault, and lists the actions that do work for a design column. The same
check runs in every mode, whether the plan came from
`propose_roles()`, a hand edit or the guided editor.

### More than one table

A confidential dataset often arrives as several related files or a
multi-sheet workbook. `masque()` handles those too. Point it at a
folder, an `.xlsx` file, or a named list of tables and it masks every
table at once, aliasing any shared key (a site code, a genotype name)
*identically across tables* so a join of the synthetic tables still works.

```{r set}
set_dir <- system.file("extdata", "met_set", package = "masque")
ms <- masque(set_dir, seed = 1L, ask = FALSE)
ms
```

The environment column `env` and the genotype column `gen` appear in both
tables and are masked to the same codes in each, so the `agronomy` and `quality` tables still join. A key shared across
tables takes a `_K` code, such as `gen_K056`.

The warning is about `year`. It is an environment column, but it is
numeric, so its real values are kept. To replace its values with codes, read the tables, convert `year` to a
factor, and mask the list:

```{r set-year}
tabs <- read_set(set_dir)
tabs$agronomy[, year := factor(year)]
ms <- masque(tabs, seed = 1L, ask = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
knitr::kable(
  head(synthetic(ms)$agronomy[, c("env", "loc", "year", "gen")], 3L),
  caption = "The first rows of the clone, with `year` now coded."
)
```

For a workbook, `sheets =` picks which sheets to read, and `info =` names
documentation sheets, such as a data dictionary, to set aside: they are
not masked and not written. See *Confidentiality and the threat model* for
the set-level controls.

### Describing the clone: the data card

A collaborator planning an analysis needs to know the shape of the data
before any code is written: how many rows, which columns are the design,
which is the outcome, how much is missing. `data_card()` writes those
facts down without a single value of any column. It reads only the clone
and its role table, which `roles()` returns in the clone's own column
names:

```{r data-card-roles}
knitr::kable(
  roles(m),
  caption = "The role table of the clone, as the data card reads it."
)
```

The role table says which columns are design columns, but not which of
them give a plot's position or identify the plot. The data owner names
those when writing the card:

```{r data-card}
card_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".yaml")
card <- data_card(
  m,
  file = card_file,
  name = "alpha_trial",
  spatial = c("row", "col"),
  unit = "plot"
)
writeLines(head(readLines(card_file), 30))
```

Further down, each column has its own entry. The entries for the
genotypes and the yields give counts and no values:

```{r data-card-gen}
card_lines <- readLines(card_file)
gen_at <- grep('name: "gen"', card_lines, fixed = TRUE)
writeLines(card_lines[gen_at + 0:24])
```

Every entry carries a provenance class. `structure` marks a count that is
exact in the clone and so equal on the real table, such as the number of
missing values or the number of genotypes. `clone_estimate` marks one
that was drawn or re-simulated, such as the number of distinct yields. `analyst`
marks what was named in the call. Level labels never appear: the card
says there are 24 genotypes and does not list them. When `alias_names = TRUE` hides the column names, the card uses the
aliases. For a set, `data_card(ms)`
returns one card per table, and `data_card(ms, file = dir)` writes one
file per table.

### Multi-environment structure

For a multi-environment trial, `detect_design()` answers three questions
separately:

1. Which rows belong to each environment?
2. Do the treatments connect the environments, so that they can be
   compared?
3. What randomisation structure can be recovered within each environment?

A block or field layout seen in the data suggests the original
randomisation but does not confirm it. A small toy with two environments
and three genotypes:

```{r met-scope}
met <- expand.grid(
  env = factor(c("E1", "E2")),
  rep = factor(seq_len(2L)),
  gen = factor(c("G1", "G2", "G3"))
)
met$yield <- seq_len(nrow(met)) + rep(c(0, 2), each = 6L)

ds <- detect_design(met)
ds@scope_label
ds@env_cols
ds@connectivity$status
ds@within_design_label
```

The toy has one environment column, `env`. The environments are connected,
and each holds a randomised complete block design (RCBD).

Automatic detection is conservative. A column named `env` or
`environment`, or a common site-year pattern, is taken as the environment
only when no other column explains the structure as well. A site column on
its own is taken only when treatments are replicated across sites, so a
nested block is not mistaken for an environment. When you know the
environment columns, name them:

```{r met-explicit}
ds_explicit <- detect_design(met, env = "env")
```

### Figure: the multi-environment coverage plot

`plot()` on the result of `detect_design()`, or `plot_design_summary()`,
draws a compact environment overview in base graphics. With
`engine = "ggplot2"` it returns a `ggplot2` object you can save with
`ggplot2::ggsave()`. Printed, it is the figure below. It shows whether
coverage is even across environments, which the connectivity flag alone
does not.

```{r met-plot, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.cap = "Treatments observed in each environment of the toy trial. The subtitle gives connectivity, the number of connected components and the design found within each environment.", fig.alt = "Bar chart: three treatments observed in each of the environments E1 and E2. The subtitle reports one connected component and an RCBD within each environment."}
plot(ds_explicit, df = met, engine = "ggplot2")
```

```{r met-plot-skip, eval = !requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("ggplot2 is not installed on this build, so the coverage figure is",
    "skipped; `plot(ds_explicit, df = met)` still draws the base-graphics",
    "equivalent.\n")
```

Both bars are at three treatments, since every genotype in this toy trial
appears in both environments. A shorter bar marks an environment with fewer treatments. A subtitle with
more than one component marks environments that share no treatments with
the rest and cannot go into one connected analysis. In either case, check
whether the gap is real or comes from how the table was assembled.

An environment column that `detect_design()` identifies with high
confidence becomes a `design` column in the plan:

* The default and collaborate modes code categorical environment labels in
  place, so each row stays in its environment and missing values stay
  where they were. The recipe turns the codes back into the real labels.
* Local mode keeps environment values byte-identical.

A numeric environment such as `year` stays at `keep`, as shown above. The
toy's `env` column is categorical:

```{r met-roles}
met_roles <- propose_roles(met)
knitr::kable(
  met_roles[met_roles$col == "env", c("col", "role", "action")],
  caption = "How the default masking plan treats the `env` column."
)
```

This safeguard protects the allocation a pipeline reads. A default clone
carries no genotype-by-environment effect at all. A local or collaborate
clone carries one only when it is conditional, and even then sparse
treatment-by-environment cells may fall back to pooled synthesis. No clone
is a substitute for the original trial in scientific inference.

## Results

```{r audit-tally, include = FALSE}
audit <- audit_mask(m, print = FALSE)
grades <- c(audit$leakage_class, attr(audit, "joint")$leakage_class)
n_high <- sum(grades == "high")
n_medium <- sum(grades == "medium")
```

On this trial the audit of the default clone, counting its per-column and whole-table checks together, gave `r n_high` HIGH and `r n_medium` medium
findings. A HIGH finding would stop the package writing the synthetic to
disk. The plot layout comes back unchanged, the replicate and block labels
come back as codes, the genotypes come back as `trt_001` to `trt_024`, and
each yield lies between the 1st and 99th percentiles of the real yields. A
plan that asks for something the package will not do is refused before it
runs. Related tables are masked together and still join.

The agronomist can therefore hand over a default clone that keeps the plot
layout and the links between tables, and only a coarse summary of the real
yields. The statistician can write and run a full pipeline on it without
seeing the real genotype names or yields. A collaborate clone adds the
correlations between numeric columns, and `conditional = TRUE` adds the
treatment effect. `handover()` writes the clone, its plan and its data
card to a folder for the collaborator. How the
finished pipeline runs on the real data is covered in *Recipe anatomy and
the round-trip*.

## Limits

This vignette shows the data owner's side of the handover, on one small
public trial with a clean, complete design. It does not exercise the
leakage audit's failure modes, the coordinate controls or the conditional
clone, which are all in *Confidentiality and the threat model*. A
sensitive column with an ordinary name is caught only if someone flags it
by hand. Multi-environment detection can miss a real environment when the
names and replication are ambiguous, so name `env` explicitly when you
know it. The trial has only one numeric
outcome, so the vignette does not show what the Gaussian copula of local
and collaborate mode keeps of the relationships between columns. That is
also in *Confidentiality and the threat model*.

## What to read next

*Confidentiality and the threat model* sets out what a synthetic
clone protects and what it does not, the depth controls beyond role and
action, the leakage audit, and the conditional clone that mimics a
treatment effect. *Recipe anatomy and the round-trip* is the analyst's
side of this handover: what the recipe carries, and how a pipeline built on
the synthetic runs on the original. *What a
conditional clone keeps of the design* tests what a model fitted on a
conditional clone still finds, on eight field designs. *Known-truth controls* derives
datasets in which the answer is known, to check a pipeline before it meets
the real data.

## Reproduce

`set.seed(1)` is set once for the document, and every `masque()` or
`mask()` call passes its own seed, so each is reproducible on its own.
Package versions follow.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```

## References

John, J. A., & Williams, E. R. (1995). *Cyclic and computer generated
designs* (2nd ed.). Chapman and Hall.
